blocks.title: Chapter VII Privacy and Confidentiality
blocks.content:
Privacy and Confidentiality
© WHO
142
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality
Privacy and confidentiality – the first an interest or right 
of either individuals or small groups of people, and the 
second a duty of professionals – might be jeopardized by 
health research. When privacy and confidentiality can be 
fully protected without the scientific value of the research 
being compromised, scientists clearly have a duty to do so, 
barring specific obstacles. In some cases, conflicts between 
the interests of science and part

summary.text: Opens the chapter on privacy and confidentiality in a casebook on ethical issues in international health research, contrasting privacy as an interest of individuals or groups with confidentiality as a professional duty. It outlines three kinds of privacy interest (control over access to information, over being observed, and over personal decisions) and notes that what counts as an intrusion differs between cultures. It explains why both tangible interests, such as employment or insurance, and intangible ones, such as dignity and the shaping of relationships, deserve protection, and how research ethics committees should weigh risks against the value of the knowledge sought. The section ends by warning that whole communities can be stigmatized by research findings or by disclosing study sites, followed by suggested readings on returning individual results and on data protection.

blocks.title: Case 46. Studying Nevirapine in West Africa
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality
A study in a West African country is designed to examine the 
effectiveness of the antiretroviral drug, Nevirapine, when 
administered to HIV-positive women during labour and then 
to their newborns for the first three months after birth. The 
aim of the study is to assess whether Nevirapine can reduce 
the perinatal transmission of HIV infection in infants aged 
younger than one year.
Pregnant women have their blood drawn and tested for HIV 
in the latter stages of pregnancy. They are a

summary.text: Presents a case from a West African study of nevirapine to prevent perinatal HIV transmission, in which an HIV-positive woman, one of several wives, refuses to let the doctor tell her husband for fear of being expelled or harmed. Colleagues disagree on whether the promised confidentiality should be broken, and the questions ask whether the husband or other partners should be told and whether a safety plan is owed to the woman.

blocks.title: Case 47. The quality of care in a family welfare programme
blocks.content:
in one of the states of a South Asian country. The project is 
funded by a grant from a European university to the South 
Asian university which employs the researchers. As part of 
the evaluation process, the investigators plan to interview 
the doctors, supervisors, and multipurpose health workers 
employed at selected primary health centres (PHCs) in the 
state, and the family-planning clients who visit those PHCs. 
Client-provider interactions at the centres, and at a sterili-
zation camp organized by one of the selected PHCs, will be 
observed for one week.
An ethical review board, conven

summary.text: Presents a case on evaluating care in a South Asian family welfare programme, where an ethics board required that primary health centres and staff not be identifiable, and a field researcher saw syringes being reused. After she reported it anonymously to a supervisor, she saw the same practice a week later, and the questions ask whether confidentiality should be strictly upheld and what the principal investigator should do.

blocks.title: Case 48. Responding when study findings are challenged
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality
A team of university researchers have completed an evalua-
tion of the quality of care in a family welfare programme of 
a state in a South Asian country. The researchers complied 
with the recommendations of a research ethics committee 
that they should ensure the confidentiality of all identifying 
data about the primary health centres (PHCs) – which deliver 
the programme – and their employees: all information which 
could later be used by authorities to identify specific PHCs 
or emp

summary.text: Presents a related case in which researchers who found widely varying quality of care, and poor conditions at sterilization camps, in a South Asian state's primary health centres refused officials' demands to name the centres, citing the agreed anonymity. Officials accused them of fabricating evidence and argued confidentiality did not apply, and the questions ask whether the centres should be named and when confidentiality promises may be set aside.

blocks.title: Case 49. Determining post-abortion complication levels
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality ❚
An eastern European country has passed a law to make 
abortion legal for a range of social and medical indications. 
Nevertheless, legal abortion centres are neither geographi-
cally accessible, nor always functioning effectively. Indeed, 
abortions outside of the legally recognized sector are 
still estimated to occur between two and five times more 
frequently than do those in legally recognized centres.
Although the demographic profile of abortion-seekers, 
the dangers associated with

summary.text: Presents a case on a study in an Eastern European country, where many abortions still occur outside legal centres, designed to measure post-abortion complications and link them to the type of provider across 140 villages. Women are found through providers, community health workers and women's groups, give oral consent, and are interviewed at home with safeguards such as dummy interviews, a focus on general gynaecological health and artificial privacy. One member of the funder's ethics committee doubts that identifying records will stay confidential, and the questions ask whether recruitment, oral consent and the interview methods adequately protect privacy and avoid coercion.

blocks.title: Case 50. Evaluating the cost-benefit ratio of long-term care services
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality ❚
The mental health institute of a Central American country 
has historically offered financial support to community 
mental health centres (CMHCs) that provide care for people 
who have severe, chronic mental illness (including most 
individuals with schizophrenia, and many who suffer from 
manic-depressive illness and chronic major depression). The 
institute has given this support in the form of reimburse-
ments to CMHCs for long-term care services, which typically 
include supervision

summary.text: Presents a case in which a Central American mental health institute, seeking to compare the cost and benefit of long-term community care services, told centres to obtain patients' consent to release confidential psychiatric records and to reimburse care only for those who signed. Clinicians called this coercive and objected to government access to records, and the questions ask when state access to medical records is acceptable and what makes consent valid.

blocks.title: Case 51. Research on an identifiable population
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality
A team of molecular biology researchers wishes to study 
the basis of alcoholism in selected native peoples of North 
America. This research is based on reports of a significant 
correlation between alcoholism and several forms of brain-
wave activity that are measurable by electroencephalography: 
Caucasian and African Americans with these brainwave 
patterns have a higher risk of alcoholism. There is also some 
evidence of a genetic linkage between the brainwaves and 
traits of alcohol

summary.text: Presents a case in which researchers plan to study a genetic link between brainwave patterns and alcoholism in 300 families of a North American indigenous tribe, offering payment, and many individuals want to take part. A tribal representative body urges the ethics committee to reject the study for lack of consultation, disregard for beliefs about the sacredness of blood and the risk of stigma, and the questions ask how the committee should weigh community and individual views.

blocks.title: Case 52. Case-control study of vasectomy and prostate cancer
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality ❚
Epidemiologists in an industrialized country propose to 
investigate the association between vasectomy and adeno-
carcinoma1 of the prostate gland, using a case-control study 
design. Men with prostate cancer, confirmed by histologi-
cal examination, will be identified through their clinicians’ 
records. The control group, consisting of men of similar ages 
who do not have prostate cancer, will be chosen at random 
from the national election registry. Since the country in 
question has g

summary.text: Presents a case-control study in an industrialized country on vasectomy and prostate cancer, in which cases are identified from clinicians' records, controls are drawn from the electoral register, and participants are interviewed by telephone. To avoid bias, men would be told only that the study concerns risk factors for prostate disease, and the questions ask whether record access without permission, telephone consent and withholding the study's purpose are acceptable.

blocks.title: Case 53. Studying health-seeking behaviour
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality
A team of social scientists concerned with improvement of 
women’s health wants to learn why women do not return to 
the hospital for the results of Papanicolaou (Pap) tests.1 They 
have a research project to follow up with women who have a 
presumptive diagnosis of cervical cancer (a positive Pap test) 
but who do not return to the hospital, as advised, to receive 
their test results. The aim of the research is to find out how to 
improve services to these women.
The chiefs of service i

summary.text: Presents a case in which social scientists, with hospital permission, use records to find women with positive Pap tests who did not return for results, visit them at home, give them their results and refer them directly to physicians. They justify this by the health benefits and the hospital's ownership of records, and the questions ask whether confidentiality is breached and how else the problem could have been approached.

blocks.title: Case 54. Health promotion survey research on a commercial farm
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality ❚
A large farm in southern Africa recruits both men and women 
as seasonal labourers from the nearby town, local villages and 
other rural areas. The male-female ratio among the seasonal 
labourers is approximately four to one, although other women 
are involved informally in the economy of the farm selling 
vegetables, game meat, tea, wine, and beer to farm workers in 
and around the farm. Most of the women employed as seasonal 
workers are younger than 25 years, and 70% are single.
Only

summary.text: Presents a case set on a commercial farm in southern Africa, where mostly male migrant seasonal workers live in compounds with few women, and health promotion researchers returned for a follow-up survey after agreeing their role with management and workers. Mapping showed hidden sexual contact between migrant men and local women, and registration revealed that about 8% of workers were under 16, most of them local girls aged 8 to 15. The researchers feared these girls faced sexually transmitted infections including HIV and were missing school, and the questions ask whether they should inform management and what obligations they have to protect participants.

blocks.title: Case 55. Interviewing child domestic helpers in sub-Saharan Africa

THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Privacy and Conﬁdentiality ❚
including the risk of harassment or a beating, the children 
will be interviewed in private. Each interviewer will have a 
separate “safe” questionnaire to revert to should the child’s 
“employer” enter the room unexpectedly, and the child will 
have been prepared for this possibility. The interviewers will 
give the children their contact details and information about 
how to contact a psychologist who is working on the study 
with them. Both the employers and the house helpers will be

summary.text: Presents Case 55, a questionnaire study of reproductive health problems among girls aged 13–17 who live away from home as domestic workers in sub-Saharan Africa, set against the background of child fosterage being misused for trafficking. It describes how households are approached, how children give consent and are interviewed privately with a decoy questionnaire, contact details and compensation, and then asks whether privacy, safety and valid consent have been adequately addressed.

blocks.title: Chapter VIII Professional Ethics
blocks.content:
Chapter VIII

160
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics
The expectation that researchers and other stakeholders in 
the research process – including ethics committee members, 
sponsors, and funders – will act with integrity and honesty 
is a fair one. When a research article is published, it is fair to 
expect, at the very least, that the data has not been fabricated, 
falsified, or plagiarized; that results are correctly reported; 
that the disclaimers about conflicts of interest are complete 
and correct; that a thorough and

summary.text: Opens the chapter on professional ethics in a casebook on ethical issues in international health research, setting out what can fairly be expected of researchers, ethics committee members, sponsors and funders in terms of integrity and honesty. It focuses on two broad areas, conflicts of interest and scientific misconduct, defining a conflict of interest as a situation where personal gain could compromise duties to participants or to sound science, and separating this from the tension between patient care and good science. It explains how industry-funded research and scientists' financial ties to companies have made such conflicts widespread, and discusses concerns about commercial research ethics committees and fees charged by committees. The section closes with suggested readings on industry relationships, whistleblowing and cross-cultural views of scientific misconduct.

blocks.title: Case 56. Testing delivery methods for a hormonal contraceptive
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics ❚
The manufacturer of a new hormonal contraceptive commis-
sions a research team to design a clinical trial to compare the 
effectiveness and tolerability of the new preparation using 
three different methods of delivery – oral tablets, transder-
mal patches, and injections. The manufacturer also wants the 
researchers to focus on the use of this new contraceptive in 
women of two different socioeconomic groups. The working 
hypothesis is that the delivery of hormonal contraceptives by 
transderm

summary.text: Case 56 describes a manufacturer-sponsored trial comparing tablet, patch and injectable forms of a new hormonal contraceptive in women from two socioeconomic groups, with the company paying researchers' salaries, computers and a per-participant fee and giving volunteers a small payment. Questions ask about the appropriateness of these benefits, conflicts of interest, partner involvement in consent, infections acquired during the trial and the sponsor's obligations if the product fails.

blocks.title: Case 57. Testing a treatment for schizophrenia
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics
An Asian pharmaceutical company has developed a prom-
ising new antipsychotic medication for the treatment of 
 schizophrenia.1 Sales analysts predict the drug could earn the 
company a substantial profit within four years. The study drug 
has already been tested on several thousand volunteers in Asia. 
During this testing, however, some study participants devel-
oped cardiac arrhythmias. Consequently, the regulatory agency 
responsible issued a “not approvable” letter, which requires the 
drug

summary.text: Case 57 describes an Asian drug company that, after a regulator refused approval of its antipsychotic over heart rhythm problems, contracts an overcrowded eastern European psychiatric hospital to test it, with doctors paid per recruited patient and local regulators not told of the earlier refusal. Questions cover risk-benefit, disclosure duties across countries, ensuring capacity to consent, possible misconduct, recruiters' conflicts of interest and post-trial access.

blocks.title: Case 58. Budget reviews by research ethics committees
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics ❚
A major North American university has submitted a research 
proposal to the research ethics committee of the National 
University School of Medicine (NUSM) in a developing coun-
try in South-East Asia. It is an ambitious proposal that carries 
with it a US$ 500 000 yearly budget to examine the efficacy 
of an innovative national family planning programme The 
proposal includes bringing researchers to North America for 
short-term training on new family planning strategies, low-
cost surgeries,

summary.text: Case 58 describes a research ethics committee at a South-East Asian medical school that refuses to review a large North American family planning study unless it sees the budget, while the North American university fears the school's 10% overhead could sway members who are also on the research team. Questions ask whether budget review belongs to an ethics committee, how any conflict of interest could be handled and how capacity-building benefits should be weighed.

blocks.title: Case 59. Determining the workforce costs of the AIDS epidemic
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics
The staff-benefits group of a west African mining company 
asks a research team based at a European university to help 
determine the economic impact of the AIDS epidemic on their 
workforce. The group wants to convince senior management 
that the cost is much higher than expected. They suspect that 
absenteeism due to AIDS, rapid turnover of highly trained 
and semi-skilled staff (which generates retraining costs), 
treatment costs associated with the illness, and one-time 
benefits and funera

summary.text: Case 59 describes a European university team, fully funded by a west African mining company, studying the cost of AIDS to the company's workforce in the hope of prompting prevention programmes. A trade union official warns that the company may instead dismiss HIV-positive workers or downsize, and the company refuses to give written assurances. After the findings show rising health care costs, the chief executive asks the team to recommend capping HIV insurance benefits, and questions ask how researchers should guard against misuse of their data and respond to such pressure.

blocks.title: Case 60. Action research on involuntary resettlement
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics
A small community-based NGO has been delivering a health 
programme in the slums of a large city in South Asia. Part 
of the slum’s population has been relocated to another 
colony, 15 km away, and the NGO has set up a clinic in this 
new colony. Based on their experience with the community 
both before and after relocation, the NGO staff members are 
convinced that the process of resettlement has damaged 
even further the lives of the people who have been relocated. 
To expose the living condi

summary.text: Case 60 describes a small NGO in a South Asian city that partners with a research organization to study how relocation from slums to a distant colony has affected people's health, education and livelihoods. The ethics committee bars recruiting case-study participants from the NGO's clinic users for fear they would feel coerced, so the team runs a random household survey, but by identifying with the NGO it faces pressure to give direct help and participants expect services. Questions concern the committee's decision, how far to meet community expectations, effects on informed consent and the tension between action and research.

blocks.title: Case 61. Victimizing the system or a victim of it?
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics
Xue Lee, a 25-year-old research assistant with plans to go to 
medical school, has discovered that a set of data given to her 
by a much-admired senior researcher, Dr Simpson, does not 
support the working hypothesis of their lab, which is that the 
increased vulnerability to cardiovascular disease that accom-
panies ageing is due to changes in the ratio of different levels 
of lipids or fats in the blood.
Ms Lee shows the unexpected results to Dr Simpson, who 
takes the file home with him to r

summary.text: Case 61 describes a young research assistant who finds that a respected senior researcher altered data that contradicted their lab's hypothesis, and then uncovers a wider pattern of fabricated measurements and non-existent patients. Despite a colleague's warning that everyone will lose, she files a formal complaint, and an inquiry leads the researcher, a major grant earner, to plead guilty to falsifying a federal grant application after more than a decade of fraud. Questions ask whether his pleas for leniency are valid, how whistle-blowers should be treated and who should enforce scientific integrity.

blocks.title: Case 62. Truth and consequences
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
❚ THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics
Six graduate students who work under Professor Maria Kieros 
in the department of genetics at a major university have 
reluctantly come to the conclusion that she has been faking 
data. This conclusion is based on a number of direct and indi-
rect observations. In reading a grant application, for example, 
Ms Heath, one of the graduate students, has noted that some 
data was represented as if it were unpublished data even 
though it had appeared in an earlier paper published by the 
laboratory.

summary.text: Case 62 describes six genetics graduate students who suspect their professor of faking data, confront her, and after months of hesitation over the risk to their own research report her to the university. An investigation finds falsified grant applications and pressure on students to hide unwanted results, and after the professor resigns most students must restart their projects, leave or face years of delay. Questions ask whether they should have reported, what would have happened had they stayed silent and how universities should protect whistle-blowers.

blocks.title: Case 63. The curious career of Dr Taylor
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics ❚
For almost three decades, Dr Taylor had a prosperous career 
at a well-respected North American university, during which 
he became a world-renowned expert in the fields of nutri-
tion and immunology. He was often nominated for, and had 
received, prestigious awards and recognitions.
While at the university, Dr Taylor was asked by a company 
based in the United States of America, Blake Pharmaceuticals, 
to undertake a large study to test whether their new infant 
formula could help babies avoid

summary.text: Case 63 describes a renowned nutrition researcher whose infant formula studies, involving hundreds of supposed babies, are found by an independent panel to have never been carried out, yet his university takes no action after he threatens to sue. He goes on to publish an implausible study of his own patented multivitamin and memory in older people, later supported only by an untraceable author in his own journal, and he retires to promote the product. Questions ask about the university's duties, whether an ethics committee may weigh a researcher's credibility, and the roles of government, professional societies and journals in addressing fraud.

blocks.title: Case 64. Whose idea is it, anyway?
blocks.content:
CASEBOOK ON ETHICAL ISSUES IN INTERNATIONAL HEALTH RESEARCH
THE CASE STUDIES ❚ Professional Ethics ❚
Dr Ruiz is a very productive physician-scientist at a Central 
American medical research institute in country A, and has 
completed more than 15 studies and published more than 
20 papers. More than 70% of the protocols he has submit-
ted for funding have been approved and implemented. After 
5 years, he returns to his home country (country B, also in 
Central America), leaving behind several ongoing, unfinished 
studies in the hands of his co-investigators. He also leaves 
behind unfunded prot

summary.text: Case 64 describes a Central American physician-scientist who, asked by an international funder to review a proposal, recognises it as a near copy of an unfunded protocol he wrote with co-investigators at his former institute in another country. The funder rejects the proposal but, after an internal review that never contacts him, finds only possible negligence and treats the protocol as public domain. Questions ask whether the matter was handled fairly, whether a different standard applied to a developing-country researcher, which ethical standards apply, and who owns research ideas and deserves authorship.

blocks.title: Appendix
blocks.content:
The ethical principles included here are reprinted from the 
International Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research Involving 
Human Subjects, prepared by the Council for International 
Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) in collaboration 
with the World Health Organization.1 While these principles 
are widely known and referred to, it is important to recognize 
that there are additional and alternative principles that provide 
useful conceptual and practical frameworks.
GENERAL ETHICAL PRINCIPLES
All research involving human subjects should be conducted 
in accordance with three basic

summary.text: The appendix of the Casebook reprints the general ethical principles from the CIOMS International Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research Involving Human Subjects, noting that other principles also offer useful frameworks. It sets out respect for persons, covering autonomy and protection of those with diminished autonomy, beneficence, including non-maleficence, and justice, understood mainly as fair distribution of the burdens and benefits of research with special protection for vulnerable people. It adds that research should leave low-resource countries no worse off, respond to their health needs and use the least vulnerable participants necessary, and closes with the ISBN and a note that the publication came from a WHO Research Ethics Review Committee project with the University of Geneva.
